subject: physics
question_text: Distinguish between streamline flow and turbulent flow of liquids.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 Short Answer Question 5 (printed p.108), printed again word for word as Long Answer Question 2 (printed p.111). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 8-mark and 4-mark splits are both INVENTED and are a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them. Physics hand-checked: streamline flow has every particle repeat the same path and velocity at a fixed point and occurs below the critical velocity; turbulent flow has paths that cross and change with time and occurs above it; the Reynolds number Re = ρvD/η (D the tube diameter) decides which regime occurs, with streamline flow below about Re = 1000 and turbulent flow above about Re = 2000.

cuts.label: Long answer — 8 marks
cuts.note: The full question as the paper asks it: both definitions, all four contrasts, the Reynolds number and an example. The 8-mark split is a claim.

cuts.label: Short answer — 4 marks

s3_contrast_path.margin_note: First mark. State both sides, one path repeated, against paths that cross and change.

s4_contrast_velocity.margin_note: Second mark. Steady at a point, against irregular at a point.

s5_contrast_critical_velocity.margin_note: Third mark. Below or above the critical velocity, and name the Reynolds number as the deciding factor.

s6_contrast_energy.margin_note: Fourth mark. Little loss, against energy lost into eddies and heat.

cuts.note: Sri Chaitanya Fastrack SHORT ANSWER form of the same question, four marks. Keeps the four contrasts and drops the two definitions, the Reynolds expression and the example; the four-mark split is invented.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Define streamline flow
lines: Every particle passing a fixed point
follows the same path as the particle
before it, with the same velocity.
This is also called laminar flow. It
occurs when the flow speed is below the
critical velocity of the liquid.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name streamline flow and say the path and velocity repeat at each point.
steps.why: This single trait, a fixed path and a fixed velocity at each point, is what every contrast below is measured against.
common_mistakes: Saying the particles all move at the same speed as each other, rather than each one repeating the same speed at that point.
Leaving out that it occurs below the critical velocity.

recall.must_convey: That in streamline flow every particle passing a point follows the same path with the same velocity, below the critical velocity.
accept: streamline flow, same path same velocity
every particle follows the same path at a point
laminar flow, below the critical velocity

steps.memory_tip: Streamline: same path, same speed, every particle, every time.

steps.label: Define turbulent flow
lines: The paths of particles cross one another
and change from moment to moment. Small
whirls called eddies form, and the flow
becomes irregular.
It occurs when the flow speed is above
the critical velocity.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name turbulent flow and say the paths cross and change; above the critical velocity.
steps.why: Turbulent flow is defined by the same two traits failing, no fixed path and no fixed velocity, so stating it right after streamline flow makes the contrast visible at once.
common_mistakes: Describing turbulence only as messy or disordered flow, without saying the paths cross and change with time.
Saying it occurs below the critical velocity. Turbulent flow is above it.

recall.must_convey: That in turbulent flow the paths of particles cross and change from moment to moment, with eddies, above the critical velocity.

steps.memory_tip: Turbulent: paths tangle, eddies form, above the critical velocity.

steps.label: Contrast: path of particles
lines: In streamline flow, every particle
passing a given point follows the same
path with the same velocity as the
particle before it.
In turbulent flow, the paths of
particles cross one another and change
from moment to moment.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. State both sides, one path repeated, against paths that cross and change.
steps.why: This is the clearest test: watch one point and see whether every particle that passes it repeats the same path, or a different one each time.
common_mistakes: Describing only streamline flow and leaving turbulent flow unstated.
Saying the paths are random without saying they cross and change.

recall.must_convey: That streamline flow has every particle repeat the same path and velocity at a point, while turbulent flow has paths that cross and change moment to moment.
accept: streamline keeps one path, turbulent paths cross
same path and velocity against crossing changing paths
particles repeat the same path in streamline flow
path contrast, streamline same, turbulent changes
one is a fixed path, the other keeps crossing
reject: velocity at a point is steady or irregular
energy is carried forward or lost to eddies

steps.memory_tip: One path repeated is streamline. Crossing, changing paths is turbulent.

steps.label: Contrast: velocity at a point
lines: In streamline flow, the velocity at each
point stays steady with time.
In turbulent flow, the velocity at a
point varies irregularly from one
instant to the next.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Steady at a point, against irregular at a point.
steps.why: This is a test at ONE fixed point over time, different from the path test, which compares different particles passing that point.
common_mistakes: Repeating the path contrast instead of talking about the velocity AT a point over time.
Saying the velocity is zero in turbulent flow rather than irregular.

recall.must_convey: That in streamline flow the velocity at a point stays steady with time, while in turbulent flow it varies irregularly.
accept: velocity at a point is steady in streamline flow
turbulent flow, velocity keeps changing at a point
steady velocity against irregular velocity
velocity contrast, steady versus irregular
at a fixed point the speed does not change in streamline flow
reject: same path with the same velocity as the particle before it
the Reynolds number decides which occurs

steps.memory_tip: Steady velocity at a point is streamline. Flickering velocity is turbulent.

steps.label: Contrast: critical velocity
lines: Streamline flow occurs only below the
critical velocity of the liquid.
Turbulent flow occurs above it.
Which one occurs is decided by the
Reynolds number, a number found from the
density, speed, tube size and viscosity
of the liquid.
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Below or above the critical velocity, and name the Reynolds number as the deciding factor.
steps.why: The critical velocity is the actual boundary between the two flows, and the Reynolds number is the rule that fixes where that boundary lies for a given liquid and tube.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the Reynolds number entirely.
Reversing the direction. Turbulent flow is above the critical velocity, not below.

recall.must_convey: That streamline flow is below the critical velocity and turbulent flow is above it, and that the Reynolds number decides which occurs.
accept: below critical velocity streamline, above turbulent
the Reynolds number decides streamline or turbulent
critical velocity is the boundary between the two

streamline below, turbulent above the critical speed
reject: little energy is lost in streamline flow
the paths cross and change from moment to moment

steps.memory_tip: Below critical velocity, streamline. Above it, turbulent. Reynolds number decides.

steps.label: Contrast: energy loss
lines: In streamline flow, the kinetic energy
of the liquid is carried forward with
little loss.
In turbulent flow, much of the energy is
lost to the eddies and converted into
heat.
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Little loss, against energy lost into eddies and heat.
steps.why: This is why the distinction matters in practice: a turbulent flow needs more pumping energy to carry the same liquid the same distance.
common_mistakes: Saying no energy at all is lost in streamline flow. It is only a SMALL loss, not zero.
Not naming where the lost energy goes, into eddies and heat.

recall.must_convey: That streamline flow carries its kinetic energy forward with little loss, while turbulent flow loses much of its energy to eddies and heat.

turbulent flow loses energy to eddies and heat

steps.memory_tip: Streamline carries energy forward. Turbulent spends it on eddies and heat.

steps.label: Reynolds number
lines: The Reynolds number Re decides which
kind of flow occurs, for a liquid of
density ρ and viscosity η moving with
speed v through a tube of diameter D:
Re is a pure number, with no unit.
Flow is streamline for Re below about
1000, and turbulent for Re above about
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Write the expression and name every symbol; give the two rough limits.
steps.why: This step gives the actual rule behind the fifth mark: the single number that combines density, speed, tube size and viscosity into the streamline-or-turbulent test.
common_mistakes: Writing the wrong symbol for one of the four quantities in Re.
Giving a single sharp number instead of the two rough limits, 1000 and 2000.

recall.must_convey: That Re = ρvD/η is a pure number, streamline below about 1000 and turbulent above about 2000.

steps.memory_tip: Re = ρvD/η. Small Re, smooth flow; large Re, turbulent flow.

steps.label: Everyday example
lines: Smoke rising from an incense stick shows
both kinds of flow.
Near the stick the smoke rises in a
smooth, streamline path.
Higher up, as its speed increases, the
path breaks into swirling turbulent
eddies.
steps.margin_note: Eighth mark. One example is enough; name where each kind of flow appears in it.
steps.why: A real, observable example is what turns the four contrasts above from abstract rules into something a student can actually watch happen.
common_mistakes: Naming an example but not saying which part is streamline and which is turbulent.
Giving an example with no visible flow, so neither kind can be pointed to.

recall.must_convey: That incense smoke rises in a smooth streamline path near the stick and turns turbulent higher up as its speed increases.
